book.title: To Protect and Serve

evidence: trade publisher signal: Pocket Books / Simon & Schuster

argument.statement: The LAPD’s aggressive policing culture and refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing helped produce the unrest following the beating of Rodney King.

book.summary: Why did the city of Los Angeles erupt in flames over the police beating of a black man named Rodney King? How could the worst American insurrection of the twentieth century take place under the nose of the most powerful and omnipresent police department in the nation? How could even Mayor Tom Bradley - a twenty-one-year veteran of the LAPD - fail to change the force's sacred credo:. Give no slack and take no shit from anyone. Confront and command. Control the streets at all times. Always be aggressive. Stop crimes before they happen. Seek them out. Shake them down. Make that arrest. And never, never admit the department has done anything wrong. Joe Domanick brings a historian's perspective and a novelist's eye to this story of the LAPD in its mythic years, a force canonized by "Dragnet" as America's Cops. He brings us the real story behind the City of Angels, first known as "Peoria with palms" and settled by the sons and daughters of the American heartland.^ In the years before World War II, James E. Davis was police chief. His blue-gray eyes stared out like two piercing bullets, leading a reporter to comment that "even if he hadn't been a policeman, you'd wonder if you had forgotten to hide the body." During his reign the LAPD began writing the book on big-muscle law enforcement. But it was his successor, William H.
